records.source: וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר׃
records.gloss: And answered Job and said:
pieces: Then Job answered:

decisions.choice: Job answers Eliphaz
decisions.reason: This is Job's reply to Eliphaz's second speech (chapter 15). As in 3:2, 9:1 and 12:1, the words that introduce a speech are prose; the speech itself (16:2-17:16) is poetry.

decisions.choice: answered (Balanced), said (Readable), without "and said"
decisions.reason: Hebrew introduces speech with two verbs, "answered and said". Literal keeps both; Balanced and Readable say it once, with the same wording at every speech introduction in Job.

records.heading: Comforters who bring trouble

records.source: שָׁמַ֣עְתִּי כְאֵ֣לֶּה רַבּ֑וֹת מְנַחֲמֵ֖י עָמָ֣ל כֻּלְּכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: I have heard like these many; comforters of trouble [are] all of you.
pieces: I have heard many things like these; \q you are all miserable comforters.

L.2: I have heard many [things] like these; \q comforters of trouble [are] all of you.

R.2: I have heard all this before. \q Some comforters you are! You only make my trouble worse.

decisions.choice: comforters of trouble: comforters who bring trouble instead of comfort
decisions.reason: The friends came "to comfort" Job (2:11), with the same verb (nacham). Their comfort only adds to his misery ('amal), the very word Eliphaz has just used of what the wicked conceive (15:35).

decisions.choice: many things like these: the same old teaching
decisions.reason: Eliphaz appealed to the wisdom handed down from the ancestors (15:17-19). Job says he has heard it all many times; it says nothing new about his case.

decisions.choice: all of you: Job now speaks to all three friends
decisions.reason: The pronoun is plural: Job answers not only Eliphaz but all three friends together.

decisions.choice: miserable comforters
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the sense of the Hebrew phrase (m1) in a natural English adjective.

decisions.choice: Some comforters you are! You only make my trouble worse.
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the sense of the phrase (m1) with an exclamation that keeps its bitter tone.

records.source: הֲקֵ֥ץ לְדִבְרֵי־ר֑וּחַ א֥וֹ מַה־יַּ֝מְרִֽיצְךָ֗ כִּ֣י תַעֲנֶֽה׃
records.gloss: [Is there] an end to words of wind? Or what provokes you that you answer?
pieces: Will these windy words never end? \q What is eating at you, that you keep answering?

L.3: [Is there] an end to words of wind? \q Or what provokes you that you answer?

R.3: Will your empty talk ever stop? \q What makes you keep on arguing?

decisions.choice: words of wind: Job throws back Eliphaz's charge
decisions.reason: Eliphaz opened by saying that Job answers with "knowledge of wind" (15:2). Job uses the same picture for the friends' words.

decisions.choice: provokes: irritates, stings
decisions.reason: The verb (marats, causative) means to irritate or pain (6:25; 1 Kings 2:8, "a painful curse"). Job asks what is bothering Eliphaz so much that he must keep talking.

decisions.choice: you: Eliphaz alone
decisions.reason: Here "you" is singular: after speaking to all three (verse 2), Job turns to Eliphaz, who has just spoken.

decisions.choice: What is eating at you
decisions.reason: Balanced uses an everyday phrase for the sense of irritation (m2).

records.source: גַּ֤ם׀אָנֹכִי֮ כָּכֶ֪ם אֲדַ֫בֵּ֥רָה ל֤וּ־יֵ֪שׁ נַפְשְׁכֶ֡ם תַּ֤חַת נַפְשִׁ֗י אַחְבִּ֣ירָה עֲלֵיכֶ֣ם בְּמִלִּ֑ים וְאָנִ֥יעָה עֲ֝לֵיכֶ֗ם בְּמ֣וֹ רֹאשִֽׁי׃
records.gloss: Also I like you would speak, if were your soul in place of my soul; I would join together against you with words, and I would shake against you with my head.
pieces: I too could talk as you do, \q if you were in my place; \q I could string words together against you \q and shake my head at you.

L.4: I also could speak like you, \q if your soul were in place of my soul; \q I could join words together against you, \q and shake my head at you.

R.4: I could talk the way you do \q if you were in my place. \q I could make fine speeches against you \q and shake my head at you.

decisions.choice: I could speak: what Job could do if their places were changed
decisions.reason: The verbs describe what Job would be able to do if he were well and one of them were suffering. It is easy, he says, to lecture someone in pain.

decisions.choice: your soul in place of my soul: if you were in my place
decisions.reason: The soul (nefesh) is the whole self. "Your self in place of my self" means "if we changed places".

decisions.choice: join words together: compose clever speeches
decisions.reason: The verb (chavar, causative) means to join or put together; here it is to string words together into a speech. A related sense, to dazzle with words, is less likely.

decisions.choice: shake my head: a gesture of scorn or of mock sympathy
decisions.reason: Shaking the head at someone in trouble is a gesture of mockery (Psalm 22:8; Lamentations 2:15; Isaiah 37:22). It may also be the empty show of sympathy that Job says the friends offer.

decisions.choice: if you were in my place
alternatives: if your soul were in place of my soul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the idiom's sense (m2); Literal keeps "soul".

records.source: אֲאַמִּצְכֶ֥ם בְּמוֹ־פִ֑י וְנִ֖יד שְׂפָתַ֣י יַחְשֹֽׂךְ׃
records.gloss: I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips would hold back.
pieces: I would encourage you with my mouth, \q and the comfort of my lips would ease your pain.

L.5: I would strengthen you with my mouth, \q and the moving of my lips would hold back [your pain].

R.5: I would use my words to make you strong. \q My comforting words would ease your pain.

decisions.choice: I would strengthen you: what a true comforter does, unlike them
alternatives: irony: I could give you mere lip service, as you give me
decisions.reason: Most likely Job says that, if their places were changed, he would really encourage them and ease their pain, unlike the friends. Some read the verse as irony that continues verse 4: Job too could offer comfort that is only words, "with the mouth" and "with the lips".

decisions.choice: the moving of my lips: words of sympathy
decisions.reason: The word (nid) comes from a verb that means to move the head in sympathy, to console (2:11 uses the verb for the friends' coming "to show sympathy"). Here it is the movement of the lips in comforting words.

decisions.choice: would hold back: would ease, with "your pain" understood
decisions.reason: The verb (chasakh) has no object here. Verse 6 uses the same verb with "my pain", which shows what is held back.

decisions.choice: your pain
decisions.reason: Every level supplies the object that verse 6 shows (m3); Literal puts it in brackets.

records.source: אִֽם־אֲ֭דַבְּרָה לֹא־יֵחָשֵׂ֣ךְ כְּאֵבִ֑י וְ֝אַחְדְּלָ֗ה מַה־מִנִּ֥י יַהֲלֹֽךְ׃
records.gloss: If I speak, not is held back my pain; and [if] I refrain, what from me goes?
pieces: If I speak, my pain is not eased; \q and if I keep silent, how much of it leaves me?

L.6: If I speak, my pain is not held back, \q and [if] I refrain, what goes away from me?

R.6: If I speak, my pain does not get any better. \q If I keep quiet, it does not go away either.

decisions.choice: my pain: his suffering of body and mind
decisions.reason: Ka'ev is pain of every kind. The narrator used the word when the friends first saw Job: "they saw that his pain was very great" (2:13).

decisions.choice: what goes from me: nothing; a question that expects the answer "none"
decisions.reason: Job asks what pain leaves him when he keeps silent. The answer is "none": neither speaking nor silence brings relief.

decisions.choice: held back: the verb of verse 5
decisions.reason: The verb (chasakh) is the same as in verse 5: Job would hold back his friends' pain if he could, but nothing holds back his own.

decisions.choice: it does not go away either
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer to the question (m2).

records.source: אַךְ־עַתָּ֥ה הֶלְאָ֑נִי הֲ֝שִׁמּ֗וֹתָ כָּל־עֲדָתִֽי׃
records.gloss: Surely now he has made me weary; you have devastated all my company.
pieces: But now God has worn me out; \q {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have laid waste my whole household.

L.7: But now {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has made me weary; \q {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have devastated all my company.

R.7: God has worn me out. \q God, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have destroyed my whole family.

decisions.choice: he ... you: Job turns from speaking about God to speaking to God
decisions.reason: The first line speaks of God as "he"; the second speaks to him as "you". Hebrew laments often move between the two (Psalm 23:2-4). From here to verse 14 Job describes how God has attacked him.

decisions.choice: my company: Job's household, his family and servants
decisions.reason: The word ('edah) is a group or community (15:34). Most likely it is everything Job lost in chapter 1: his children and his servants (1:15-19). Some take it as the circle of people around him, who have turned away (19:13-19).

decisions.choice: but now: now, in contrast
decisions.reason: The words 'akh 'attah turn from what Job could do (verses 4-6) to what has in fact happened to him.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God for the "he" of the first line, so that the reader knows who is meant (m1). Readable also names God as the "you" of the second line.

records.source: וַֽ֭תִּקְמְטֵנִי לְעֵ֣ד הָיָ֑ה וַיָּ֥קָם בִּ֥י כַ֝חֲשִׁ֗י בְּפָנַ֥י יַעֲנֶֽה׃
records.gloss: And you have shriveled me; a witness it has become; and has risen against me my leanness; to my face it testifies.
pieces: You have shriveled me up, and that has become a witness against me; \q my gauntness rises up against me \q and testifies to my face.

L.8: And {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have shriveled me up; it has become a witness, \q and my leanness has risen up against me; \q it testifies to my face.

R.8: You have made me shrivel up, \q and my thin body is like a witness who stands up and accuses me to my face.

decisions.choice: shriveled me up: made me wrinkled and wasted
decisions.reason: The verb (qamat) is rare. It most likely means to shrivel or wrinkle, which fits the leanness of the next line; in 22:16 it means "snatched away", and some take it here as "you have seized me".

decisions.choice: a witness against me: his wasted body seems to prove his guilt
decisions.reason: In a court a witness rises up to speak. Job's wasted body is like a witness against him: the friends take his suffering as proof of his sin (15:20-24). In verse 19 he will look for a witness for him in heaven.

decisions.choice: leanness: wasting, gauntness
decisions.reason: The word (kachash) usually means lying or deception (Hosea 7:3). The verb from the same root is used of flesh that grows lean (Psalm 109:24), and that sense fits here. Some take it as the lies told about Job, which also rise up against him.

decisions.choice: against me
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "against me" in the first line, which the second line makes clear.

decisions.choice: my thin body is like a witness
decisions.reason: Readable joins the picture into one line and makes it a comparison (m2).

records.source: אַפּ֤וֹ טָרַ֨ף׀וַֽיִּשְׂטְמֵ֗נִי חָרַ֣ק עָלַ֣י בְּשִׁנָּ֑יו צָרִ֓י׀יִלְט֖וֹשׁ עֵינָ֣יו לִֽי׃
records.gloss: His anger has torn [me] and he has hated me; he has gnashed at me with his teeth; my adversary sharpens his eyes at me.
pieces: His anger has torn me, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hounds me; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} grinds {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} teeth at me; \q my enemy stabs at me with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} eyes.

L.9: His anger has torn [me], and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has hated me; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has gnashed at me with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} teeth; \q my adversary sharpens {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} eyes against me.

R.9: God is so angry that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has torn me to pieces and hunts me down. \q He grinds {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} teeth at me. \q My enemy glares at me with piercing eyes.

decisions.choice: his anger: God's; Job pictures God as a wild beast
decisions.reason: No new subject is named, so "he" is still God (verse 7), and verse 11 names him. Job pictures God tearing him like a lion and baring its teeth (compare 10:16). Job means it as the bitter truth of his experience; it is not a judgment the book itself makes, for the reader knows from chapters 1-2 what Job does not.

decisions.choice: hated me: has turned on me with hostility
decisions.reason: The verb (satam) means to bear a grudge and act on it (Genesis 27:41; 50:15). Job uses it of God again in 30:21.

decisions.choice: sharpens his eyes: glares at me with eyes like blades
decisions.reason: The verb is used of sharpening a weapon. The enemy's look is as sharp as a sword.

decisions.choice: my adversary: God, as Job sees it
decisions.reason: The word (tsar) is a foe or opponent. Job has asked why God treats him as his enemy (13:24); now he calls God his adversary.

decisions.choice: God is so angry that ... and hunts me down
decisions.reason: Readable names God (m1) and says what the hostility does (m2).

records.source: פָּעֲר֬וּ עָלַ֨י׀בְּפִיהֶ֗ם בְּ֭חֶרְפָּה הִכּ֣וּ לְחָיָ֑י יַ֝֗חַד עָלַ֥י יִתְמַלָּאֽוּן׃
records.gloss: They have opened wide against me with their mouth; in scorn they have struck my cheeks; together against me they mass themselves.
pieces: People gape at me with open mouths; \q they strike my cheek in scorn; \q they gang up together against me.

L.10: They have opened wide their mouth against me; \q in scorn they have struck my cheeks; \q together they mass against me.

R.10: People open their mouths wide to sneer at me. \q They insult me and slap my face. \q They all join together against me.

decisions.choice: they: people, now joining in the attack
decisions.reason: The verbs change to the plural. Others, perhaps the friends and the crowd (19:18-19; 30:1-10), join in what God has begun. Verse 11 says God has handed Job over to them.

decisions.choice: struck my cheeks: a public insult
decisions.reason: A slap on the cheek was a grave insult (1 Kings 22:24; Lamentations 3:30; Micah 5:1).

decisions.choice: opened wide their mouth: gaping like beasts, in mockery
decisions.reason: An open mouth is a picture of jeering and of a wild animal ready to devour (Psalm 22:14; 35:21).

decisions.choice: People
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the new subject (m1).

records.source: יַסְגִּירֵ֣נִי אֵ֭ל אֶ֣ל עֲוִ֑יל וְעַל־יְדֵ֖י רְשָׁעִ֣ים יִרְטֵֽנִי׃
records.gloss: Delivers me up God to [the] unjust, and on [the] hands of [the] wicked he throws me.
pieces: God hands me over to the unjust \q and throws me into the clutches of the wicked.

L.11: God delivers me up to [the] unjust, \q and throws me into [the] hands of [the] wicked.

R.11: God has handed me over to evil people. \q He has thrown me into the power of the wicked.

decisions.choice: the unjust: wrongdoers
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word ('avil) means a young boy (21:11). With the vowels of a very similar word ('avval), it means an unjust person, which matches "the wicked" in the next line. Most read it so; read as it stands, Job is given over even to boys who mock him (19:18; 30:1).

decisions.choice: God hands me over: what the reader knows from the prologue
decisions.reason: Job says that God has given him into the power of the wicked. The reader knows that God did give Job into the Accuser's hand, though not his life (1:12; 2:6). Job knows nothing of this.

decisions.choice: throws me: casts me headlong
decisions.reason: The verb (yarat) is rare; here it means to throw someone down headlong.

records.source: שָׁ֘לֵ֤ו הָיִ֨יתִי׀וַֽיְפַרְפְּרֵ֗נִי וְאָחַ֣ז בְּ֭עָרְפִּי וַֽיְפַצְפְּצֵ֑נִי וַיְקִימֵ֥נִי ל֝֗וֹ לְמַטָּרָֽה׃
records.gloss: At ease I was, and he shattered me, and he seized [me] by my neck and he dashed me to pieces, and he set me up for himself as a target.
pieces: I was at ease, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} shattered me; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} seized me by the neck and smashed me to pieces; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} set me up as {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} target.

L.12: I was at ease, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} shattered me; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} seized [me] by my neck and dashed me to pieces; \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} set me up for {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} as a target.

R.12: I was living in peace, but God broke me apart. \q He grabbed me by the neck and smashed me to pieces. \q He has made me {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} target.

decisions.choice: at ease: secure, untroubled
decisions.reason: The word (shalev) describes a quiet, secure life. Job's life was like that before disaster struck (1:1-5; 29:2-6), though he had always feared losing it (3:25-26).

decisions.choice: shattered me; dashed me to pieces: broke me apart violently
decisions.reason: The first verb (parar, intensive form) is from the root Eliphaz used when he said Job was "doing away with" the fear of God (15:4); Job says it is God who breaks him. The second (patsats, intensive form) is used of smashing rock (Jeremiah 23:29).

decisions.choice: a target: God as an archer, Job as his mark
decisions.reason: The picture leads into verse 13. Lamentations 3:12 uses the same word: "he bent his bow and set me as a target for the arrow". Job said in 7:20, "Why have you made me your target?", with a different word.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Readable names God at the start of the verse, since the subject has not been named since verse 11.

records.source: יָ֘סֹ֤בּוּ עָלַ֨י׀רַבָּ֗יו יְפַלַּ֣ח כִּ֭לְיוֹתַי וְלֹ֣א יַחְמ֑וֹל יִשְׁפֹּ֥ךְ לָ֝אָ֗רֶץ מְרֵרָֽתִי׃
records.gloss: They surround me, his archers; he splits open my kidneys and not he spares; he pours out to the ground my gall.
pieces: His archers surround me. \q Without mercy {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} slashes open my kidneys \q and pours out my gall on the ground.

L.13: His archers surround me; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} splits open my kidneys and does not spare; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} pours out my gall on the ground.

R.13: His archers are all around me. \q Without pity {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wounds me deep inside \q and spills my insides out on the ground.

decisions.choice: his archers: those who shoot for him
decisions.reason: The word (rav) here most likely means an archer, as in Jeremiah 50:29. It is spelled like the word for "many", and some take it as "his arrows" or "his many" surrounding Job; the picture of God as an archer is the same either way.

decisions.choice: my kidneys: the vital inner organs
decisions.reason: The kidneys were thought of as the deepest part of a person; a wound there was fatal. Lamentations 3:13 says "he drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver".

decisions.choice: my gall: bile, an inner organ's fluid
decisions.reason: Merorah is gall or bile, the bitter fluid of the body (20:14, 25). To pour it on the ground is to wound a person to death.

decisions.choice: wounds me deep inside; spills my insides
alternatives: splits open my kidneys; pours out my gall
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for the organs named (m2, m3); the sense is a deep, mortal wound.

records.source: יִפְרְצֵ֣נִי פֶ֭רֶץ עַל־פְּנֵי־פָ֑רֶץ יָרֻ֖ץ עָלַ֣י כְּגִבּֽוֹר׃
records.gloss: He breaks through me [with] a breach upon [the] face of a breach; he runs against me like a warrior.
pieces: He breaks through me again and again, like a wall breached; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} charges at me like a warrior.

L.14: He breaks through me, breach upon breach; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} runs at me like a warrior.

R.14: He breaks through my defenses again and again, as an army breaks through a city wall. \q He charges at me like a soldier.

decisions.choice: breach upon breach: like a city wall broken through again and again
decisions.reason: A perets is a gap broken in a city wall during a siege (Psalm 89:41; Amos 4:3). Job pictures himself as a besieged city that God storms through one breach after another; the noun and verb are the same root.

decisions.choice: he runs against me: Job turns Eliphaz's picture around
decisions.reason: Eliphaz said that the wicked person "runs against" God like a warrior (15:26). Job uses the same verb: it is God who runs against him.

decisions.choice: a warrior: a mighty fighter
decisions.reason: The gibbor is a strong, seasoned warrior.

decisions.choice: like a wall breached (B); as an army breaks through a city wall (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the picture (m1), which the Hebrew leaves to the word "breach".

records.source: שַׂ֣ק תָּ֭פַרְתִּי עֲלֵ֣י גִלְדִּ֑י וְעֹלַ֖לְתִּי בֶעָפָ֣ר קַרְנִֽי׃
records.gloss: Sackcloth I have sewed over my skin, and I have thrust in the dust my horn.
pieces: I have sewn sackcloth over my skin \q and laid my strength in the dust.

L.15: I have sewn sackcloth over my skin, \q and thrust my horn into the dust.

R.15: I have sewn rough mourning clothes onto my skin, \q and my pride lies in the dust.

decisions.choice: sackcloth: the rough cloth worn in mourning
decisions.reason: Sackcloth was a coarse cloth, usually of goat hair, worn in grief and humiliation (Genesis 37:34; 2 Samuel 3:31). Job says he has sewn it on: he never takes it off, and it clings to his skin.

decisions.choice: my horn: my strength and dignity
decisions.reason: The horn of an animal is a picture of strength and honor (1 Samuel 2:1; Psalm 75:5-6; 89:18). To thrust it into the dust is to be brought low.

decisions.choice: thrust: pushed down, laid
decisions.reason: The verb ('alal, in a rare form) most likely means to push in or lay down. Some take it as "defiled" with dust.

decisions.choice: my strength (B); my pride (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the picture (m2); Literal keeps "horn".

decisions.choice: rough mourning clothes
decisions.reason: Readable explains what sackcloth was (m1).

records.source: פָּנַ֣י חֳ֭מַרְמְרוּ מִנִּי־בֶ֑כִי וְעַ֖ל עַפְעַפַּ֣י צַלְמָֽוֶת׃
records.gloss: My face, it is red from weeping, and on my eyelids [is] deep darkness.
pieces: My face is red with weeping, \q and deep shadows lie on my eyelids.

L.16: My face is red from weeping, \q and on my eyelids [is] deep darkness.

R.16: My face is red from crying, \q and there are dark circles around my eyes.

decisions.choice: deep darkness: dark shadows, the shadow of death
decisions.reason: The word (tsalmavet) is deep darkness, often the darkness of death (3:5; 10:21-22). Here it is the dark rings around eyes worn out by weeping, and it hints that death is near.

decisions.choice: red: flushed, inflamed
decisions.reason: The verb (chamar, in a rare intensive form) means to be red. Long weeping has left his face red and swollen.

decisions.choice: is red: the reading the scribes marked
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) give a singular verb and the reading marked in the margin (qere) a plural one, since "face" is a plural noun in Hebrew. The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: dark circles around my eyes
decisions.reason: Readable says what is seen (m1).

records.source: עַ֭ל לֹא־חָמָ֣ס בְּכַפָּ֑י וּֽתְפִלָּתִ֥י זַכָּֽה׃
records.gloss: Although not violence [is] in my palms, and my prayer [is] pure.
pieces: even though my hands have done no violence \q and my prayer is pure.

L.17: although [there is] no violence in my hands, \q and my prayer [is] pure.

R.17: And all this has happened even though I have never hurt anyone, \q and my prayers are sincere.

decisions.choice: although: in spite of
decisions.reason: The words 'al lo' mean "although not". The same words are used in Isaiah 53:9, "although he had done no violence". All of verses 12-16 happened to Job in spite of his innocence.

decisions.choice: violence: wrong done to others
decisions.reason: Chamas is violence and wrongdoing against others (Genesis 6:11). Job denies doing anyone harm.

decisions.choice: my prayer is pure: an answer to the friends
decisions.reason: Zophar told Job to put away the wrong in his hand before stretching his hands out to God (11:13-14), and Eliphaz said Job was hindering devotion (15:4). Job says his hands are clean and his prayer sincere.

decisions.choice: And all this has happened
decisions.reason: Readable makes the link to verses 12-16 plain (m1).

records.source: אֶ֭רֶץ אַל־תְּכַסִּ֣י דָמִ֑י וְֽאַל־יְהִ֥י מָ֝ק֗וֹם לְזַעֲקָתִֽי׃
records.gloss: O earth, do not cover my blood, and let not be a place for my cry.
pieces: Earth, do not cover my blood; \q let my cry find no place to rest.

L.18: Earth, do not cover my blood, \q and let there be no [resting] place for my cry.

R.18: Earth, do not hide my blood! \q Do not let my cry for justice ever be silenced.

decisions.choice: do not cover my blood: let it cry out for justice, like Abel's
decisions.reason: The blood of a murdered person cries out from the ground for justice (Genesis 4:10), and blood left uncovered is a standing accusation (Ezekiel 24:7-8; Isaiah 26:21). Job speaks as if he were already a murdered man whose death must not be forgotten.

decisions.choice: no place for my cry: let my cry never come to rest
decisions.reason: Job asks that his cry never find a place where it stops and is silenced, but go on until it is heard.

decisions.choice: my cry: an outcry for help against wrong
decisions.reason: The word (ze'aqah) is the cry of someone wronged (Genesis 18:20-21; Exodus 3:7, 9 use related words).

decisions.choice: for justice
decisions.reason: Readable says what the cry is for (m1, m3).

records.source: גַּם־עַ֭תָּה הִנֵּה־בַשָּׁמַ֣יִם עֵדִ֑י וְ֝שָׂהֲדִ֗י בַּמְּרוֹמִֽים׃
records.gloss: Also now, look, in the heavens [is] my witness, and the one testifying for me [is] in the heights.
pieces: Even now my witness is in heaven; \q the one who vouches for me is on high.

L.19: Even now, look, my witness [is] in the heavens, \q and the one who testifies for me [is] on high.

R.19: Even now I have a witness in heaven. \q There is someone on high who will speak up for me.

decisions.choice: my witness in heaven: the text leaves it open who this is
alternatives: God himself, the judge, to whom Job appeals against God the attacker
a heavenly being who takes Job's side, like the arbiter of 9:33
Job's own cry (verse 18), which rises to heaven
decisions.reason: Job does not say who his witness is. He may mean God himself: he appeals from God who attacks him (verses 7-14) to God who knows the truth, as he asks God in 17:3 to stand surety for him. Or he may hope for a heavenly figure who takes his side before God, the arbiter he said did not exist (9:33), whom he will later call his Redeemer (19:25). Some take the witness to be Job's cry, which goes up from the earth to heaven. The translation does not name him.

decisions.choice: the one who testifies for me: a word from Aramaic
decisions.reason: The second word (sahed) is the Aramaic word for a witness, found only here in the Hebrew Bible. Genesis 31:47 gives the Aramaic name of Laban's heap of witness. The two words in parallel make one picture: someone in heaven who will testify that Job is innocent.

decisions.choice: witness: a witness for him, set against the witness against him
decisions.reason: In verse 8 Job's wasted body was a witness against him. Now, even now, he says he has a witness for him in heaven.

decisions.choice: even now: in spite of everything
decisions.reason: The words "even now, look" mark a turn: with death near (verse 22), Job still holds that someone in heaven knows the truth.

decisions.choice: vouches for me
decisions.reason: Balanced uses an everyday phrase for a witness who supports someone's case. It avoids "advocate", which would suggest a lawyer, more than the word says.

records.source: מְלִיצַ֥י רֵעָ֑י אֶל־אֱ֝ל֗וֹהַ דָּלְפָ֥ה עֵינִֽי׃
records.gloss: My scorners [are] my friends; to God drips my eye.
pieces: My friends scorn me; \q my eyes pour out tears to God.

L.20: My scorners [are] my friends; \q to God my eye drips [tears].

R.20: My friends make fun of me, \q while I cry out to God with tears.

decisions.choice: my friends scorn me: the friends have become mockers
decisions.reason: The first word (melits) can mean one who mocks or one who speaks for another, an interpreter or go-between (Genesis 42:23; Job 33:23). Most likely Job says his friends mock him. Read the other way, he would be saying that his spokesman in heaven (verse 19) is his friend, who pleads for him while he weeps.

decisions.choice: my eye drips: I weep
decisions.reason: The eye dripping or pouring is a picture of tears falling without stopping (Lamentations 1:16; 3:49). Job still turns his tears toward God.

decisions.choice: My friends scorn me
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say it in natural English. Literal keeps the Hebrew phrase, which also allows the other reading (m1).

records.source: וְיוֹכַ֣ח לְגֶ֣בֶר עִם־אֱל֑וֹהַּ וּֽבֶן־אָדָ֥ם לְרֵעֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And he will argue for a man with God, and a son of man for his friend.
pieces: that he would plead for a man with God, \q as one pleads for a friend.

L.21: and [that] he would argue for a man with God, \q and [as] a son of man for his friend.

R.21: I want someone to plead my case with God, \q the way a person stands up for a friend.

decisions.choice: he would argue: the witness of verse 19 pleads Job's case
decisions.reason: The one who argues Job's case is the witness in heaven of verse 19. Who he is stays open (see verse 19). Job wants someone to stand between him and God and argue for him, as a person speaks up for a friend in court.

decisions.choice: argue: the arbiter Job longed for
decisions.reason: The verb (yakach) is the root of the word for the arbiter in 9:33: "there is no arbiter between us". What Job said there was lacking, he now hopes for.

decisions.choice: and a son of man for his friend: as a human pleads for a friend
alternatives: between a man and his friend
decisions.reason: The line most likely gives a comparison: as one person pleads for another. Some read it as part of the case: the witness would argue for Job against God and against his friends.

decisions.choice: a man: Job himself
decisions.reason: The word (gever) is a man, here Job himself, a mere human before God.

decisions.choice: he, without a capital
decisions.reason: The pronoun stands for the witness of verse 19, whose identity the text leaves open, so it is not marked as a pronoun for God.

decisions.choice: I want someone to plead my case with God
decisions.reason: Readable makes the wish plain and says "my case" for "a man" (m4).

records.source: כִּֽי־שְׁנ֣וֹת מִסְפָּ֣ר יֶאֱתָ֑יוּ וְאֹ֖רַח לֹא־אָשׁ֣וּב אֶהֱלֹֽךְ׃
records.gloss: For years of number will come, and a way [that] not I will return I will go.
pieces: For only a few years will come \q before I go the way of no return.

L.22: For [the] years of number will come, \q and I will go [the] way [from which] I will not return.

R.22: In only a few years \q I will die and never come back.

decisions.choice: years of number: few years, that can be counted
decisions.reason: Something that can be numbered is few (Deuteronomy 33:6; Isaiah 10:19). Job has only a short time left.

decisions.choice: the way of no return: death
decisions.reason: Job has spoken of going "to the land of darkness ... from which I will not return" (10:21; compare 7:9-10; 2 Samuel 12:23).

decisions.choice: for: why Job needs his witness now
decisions.reason: The verse explains Job's urgency in verses 18-21: he will soon die, so his case must be heard. The thought runs on into 17:1.

decisions.choice: I will die and never come back
decisions.reason: Readable says what the idiom means (m2).
